How it works

Drag to orbit, pinch or scroll to zoom, double-tap the view to stop following. Space bar drops.

Any 3D model can be dropped in as one mesh (STL or OBJ, binary or text). Every triangle becomes an aerodynamic element; connected, near-coplanar triangles are grouped into flat regions so a wing carved from a solid still gets a wing's pressure distribution and aspect ratio. Blunt edges with a long body behind them get the drag reduction of a reattaching wake. Raising the resolution subdivides the mesh so the local wind, and the body's spin, are sampled more finely. Mass is spread through the volume of a closed solid or over the surface of an open shell, and the inertia tensor is integrated exactly from the triangles. Nose ballast is a point mass at the model's front-most vertex.

Every built-in object is a rigid body made of small flat panels plus spheres and point masses. Each panel feels its own local wind (including the body's spin), and from that gets lift, drag, stall, and a centre of pressure that walks from the quarter chord toward mid-chord as the angle of attack grows. Separated flow also gets the wake's tipping torque, scaled by the plate's added mass, which is what makes a card flutter or tumble instead of falling flat. Tufts show the local flow and turn red where it has separated. Gliders launch at the speed where their own lift balances weight; SM is the static margin, the distance from centre of mass to neutral point in wing chords. Air density 1.225 kg/m³.
